segments.t: Boris is a comedy set behind the scenes of a television production. Alessandro, a new intern, meets the assistant director Arianna and gets a very brisk welcome. You will hear this short exchange in Italian first; do not worry about catching every word.
Tu stai fermo qui, in silenzio.
Let's go through that brief introduction. Alessandro tries to explain why he is there, but Arianna is already giving him instructions.

'Actually, I'm the intern.' The first word gently corrects her assumption. The article meaning 'the' has this form before a masculine noun beginning with an s followed by another consonant. The intern's job title has the same singular form for a man or a woman.
'I just wanted...' The past form of 'want' softens the beginning of his explanation. The final word means 'only' or 'just', but Arianna interrupts before he can say what he wanted.
'No, you don't want anything.' Italian puts a negative before 'want' and the word for 'nothing' after it. The two work together; English usually chooses 'not anything' in this sentence.
Tu stai fermo qui, in silenzio.
'You stay right here, quietly.' The description 'still' takes its ending from the man being addressed. The two words at the end literally mean 'in silence'; together they tell him not to speak.

'And you wait for instructions, okay?' Italian places the thing being awaited directly after 'wait', without a word for 'for'. These are instructions, rather than just one order; the ending on that word tells us there is more than one. Now hear the same exchange again, and follow the two speakers.
Tu stai fermo qui, in silenzio.
You have heard how to say that you are the intern, and how two negatives work together. Listen again for the short instructions; see you next time.

lines.fragment: Tu stai fermo qui, in silenzio
